config.title: Interfaces — Contracts for Objects

intro.title: Interfaces — Contracts for Objects
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple user profile system to understand how TypeScript interfaces work. You will learn that interfaces act as contracts or blueprints, defining the shape that an object must follow. The main technology you'll use is the TypeScript `interface` keyword to specify required properties and their types. By the end, you'll create objects that adhere to these interfaces, ensuring your code is more predictable and easier to debug.
intro.usecase: Interfaces act as contracts that define the shape of data structures in real-world applications. In a user dashboard, an interface ensures all user profile objects have consistent properties like name, email, and role. When building a product catalog, interfaces guarantee each product item includes required fields such as id, title, and price. This pattern is essential for API responses, form validation, and maintaining data consistency across components in large-scale applications.

objectives: Implement a TypeScript interface to define the structure of an object.
Apply an interface to enforce type safety on a function parameter.
Construct an object that adheres to a specified interface.
Update an existing interface by adding new required properties.
Manipulate an array of objects typed with an interface.
Initialize a variable with an object that satisfies multiple interfaces.
Configure optional properties within an interface definition.

steps.title: Create a TypeScript file and define a simple object
steps.instruction: Create a new TypeScript file and define a simple object with properties like name and age.
steps.hint: Start by creating an object using curly braces {} with properties and their values.
steps.seedCode: // Define a simple object with name and age properties here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a basic object defined in TypeScript with name and age properties.
successCriteria: An object is defined with at least name and age properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your object includes both name and age properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've defined an object with properties like name and age.

steps.title: Add type annotations to the object properties
steps.instruction: Add explicit type annotations to the name and age properties in your object. Make name a string and age a number.
steps.hint: In TypeScript, you can add type annotations after property names using a colon and the type (e.g., propertyName: type).
steps.expectedOutcome: The object properties should have explicit type annotations (string for name, number for age).
successCriteria: The object has type annotations: name: string and age: number.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure both properties have type annotations. Check that name is typed as string and age as number.
steps.feedbackWrong: The object properties need explicit type annotations. Add ': string' after name and ': number' after age.

steps.title: Create an interface for the object structure
steps.instruction: Create an interface named 'Person' that describes the structure of your object with the same property names and types (name: string, age: number).
steps.hint: Define an interface using the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions.
steps.expectedOutcome: An interface named Person with name (string) and age (number) properties is defined above the object.
successCriteria: The Person interface is created with correct property names and types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the interface, but check that both properties (name: string, age: number) are included with correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Person interface is missing or has incorrect structure. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword with property definitions.

steps.title: Apply the interface to your object using type annotation
steps.instruction: Add a type annotation to your person object variable using the Person interface you created.
steps.hint: After the variable name, add a colon followed by the interface name to specify its type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The person object will be explicitly typed with the Person interface, ensuring it matches the defined structure.
successCriteria: The person variable has a type annotation using the Person interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added the type annotation after the variable name, like `const person: Person = {...}`.
steps.feedbackWrong: The person object is not typed with the Person interface. Add `: Person` after the variable name.

steps.title: Create a function that accepts an object typed with your interface
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'describePerson' that takes a single parameter typed with your Person interface and returns a string describing the person.
steps.hint: Define a function with a parameter annotated with the Person interface type, then return a string that includes the person's name and age.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named 'describePerson' that accepts a Person object and returns a descriptive string.
successCriteria: The function 'describePerson' is defined, has a parameter typed with the Person interface, and returns a string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it accepts a parameter typed with the Person interface and returns a string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't defined correctly. Create a function named 'describePerson' that takes a Person parameter and returns a string.

steps.title: Call the function with your typed object
steps.instruction: Call your describePerson function with the person object and log the result to the console.
steps.hint: Use console.log() with the function call as its argument.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function is called with the typed object and its return value is logged to the console.
successCriteria: The describePerson function is called with the person object as an argument, and the result is logged using console.log().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling describePerson with the person object and logging the result with console.log().
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to call the describePerson function with the person object and log the return value.

steps.title: Extend the interface with optional properties
steps.instruction: Add an optional property called 'email' (marked with ?) to your Person interface. The property should be of type string.
steps.hint: In TypeScript, you can make a property optional by adding a question mark (?) after its name in the interface definition.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your Person interface now has an optional email property that can be used when creating person objects.
successCriteria: The Person interface includes an optional email property marked with ? and typed as string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the email property is marked as optional with ? and has the correct type (string).
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface doesn't have the optional email property yet. Remember to add 'email?: string' to your Person interface.

steps.title: Create a second object that uses the optional property
steps.instruction: Create a second object named 'personWithEmail' that conforms to your Person interface and includes the optional email property.
steps.hint: Define a new constant with the same structure as 'person' but add an email property with a string value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a second object that demonstrates using the optional property from your interface.
successCriteria: A new object named 'personWithEmail' is created with name, age, and email properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created an object, but make sure it's named 'personWithEmail' and includes all required properties plus the optional email.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating a new object with the same structure as 'person' but add an email property. Name it 'personWithEmail'.

steps.title: Call the function with both objects
steps.instruction: Call your describePerson function with both the person object and the second object you created,
steps.hint: You'll need to call describePerson twice - once with each object - and use console.log to display the returned strings.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll see two console messages: one describing Alice and one describing Bob, demonstrating that the same function works with both objects regardless of the optional email property.
successCriteria: The describePerson function is called twice with both objects, and each result is logged to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're calling describePerson with both objects and logging each result.
steps.feedbackWrong: call describePerson with both the person and personWithEmail objects, then log each result.

steps.title: log each result to the console
steps.instruction: log each result to the console.
steps.hint: You'll need to call describePerson twice - once with each object - and use console.log to display the returned strings.
steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Create a readonly property in the interface
steps.instruction: Add a readonly property called 'id' to your Person interface and demonstrate it cannot be reassigned by trying to modify it in your code.
steps.hint: Use the readonly modifier before the property name in your interface, then try to change the id value on one of your person objects.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your Person interface will have a readonly id property, and you'll see a TypeScript error if you try to reassign it.
successCriteria: The Person interface includes a readonly id property, and there's an attempt to modify it that causes a TypeScript error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added the id property, but it might not be marked as readonly, or you might not have demonstrated the reassignment restriction. Make sure to use the readonly modifier and try changing the id value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Person interface doesn't have a readonly id property, or the demonstration of immutability is missing. Add readonly id: string to the interface and attempt to modify it.
